assessment:
In this study, Debaenst and colleagues establish a semi-high throughput zebrafish crispant screening platform for rapid functional validation of candidate genes associated with heritable fragile bone disorders (FBDs). The authors selected ten genes spanning a phenotypic spectrum from severe monogenic osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) to multifactorial osteoporosis, aiming to demonstrate the utility of F0 mosaic zebrafish for skeletal disease gene validation. Using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis, they generated crispants for six OI-associated genes (CREB3L1, MBTPS2, SPARC, SERPINF1, IFITM5, SEC24D) and four osteoporosis-associated genes identified through GWAS (ALDH7A1, ESR1, DAAM2, SOST). The work addresses an important methodological gap in skeletal genetics, as traditional stable knockout lines require 6-9 months to generate, whereas crispants can be phenotyped at 3 months, enabling more rapid and cost-effective screening.

The technical execution of the CRISPR approach is robust, with next-generation sequencing confirming high indel efficiency (mean 88%, range 71-96%) and out-of-frame rates of 49-73%, resulting in 60-92% of reads predicted to cause loss-of-function. Off-target analysis demonstrated minimal unintended mutagenesis. The authors employed a comprehensive multi-stage phenotyping strategy, examining skeletal development at larval stages (7 and 14 dpf) through osteoblast imaging and mineralization staining, molecular profiles via RT-qPCR of osteogenic markers, and adult skeletal morphology (90 dpf) through Alizarin Red staining and microCT analysis. The most compelling findings emerged from adult crispants, where all tested genes except daam2 displayed consistent skeletal abnormalities including vertebral fractures, fusions, and arch malformations. Notably, aldh7a1 and mbtps2 crispants exhibited severe early lethality, while surviving adults showed dramatic skeletal defects. MicroCT analysis revealed quantitative alterations in vertebral parameters, with osteoporosis-associated genes (daam2, esr1, sost) paradoxically showing increased tissue mineral density—a finding that may inform the directionality of genetic effects at these loci.

The larval phenotypes proved more variable and less penetrant than adult phenotypes, with reviewers noting concerns about the lack of normalization to body size and the potential confounding effects of developmental timing differences. The molecular data from RT-qPCR revealed consistent downregulation of the mature osteoblast marker bglap and upregulation of col1a1a across most crispants, suggesting a shift toward immature osteoblast populations. However, the interpretation of these findings is complicated by the use of whole-body samples rather than bone-specific tissue, and the potential influence of genetic compensation mechanisms that may differentially affect larval versus adult phenotypes. The authors acknowledge that crispant mosaicism, allele heterogeneity, and maternally-deposited RNAs contribute to phenotypic variability, particularly at early developmental stages. While the study demonstrates reproducibility across independent clutches for adult phenotypes, the incomplete characterization of gene-specific features (such as maternal transcript deposition or susceptibility to genetic compensation) limits the ability to predict which candidate genes will yield robust crispant phenotypes.

Despite these limitations, the work makes a valuable contribution to skeletal genetics methodology by demonstrating that crispant screening can successfully identify skeletal phenotypes for all ten tested genes, validating their roles in bone biology. The platform combines multiple complementary approaches—morphological, histological, molecular, and quantitative imaging—to provide multidimensional phenotypic assessment. The finding that adult phenotypes are more consistent and penetrant than larval phenotypes is an important practical consideration for future screening efforts. The study also reveals unexpected biology, such as the early-onset skeletal abnormalities in osteoporosis-associated gene crispants and the increased tissue mineral density in several osteoporosis gene knockdowns, challenging assumptions about late-onset disease mechanisms. While the authors appropriately position this as a pilot study and methods paper, additional work is needed to establish guidelines for gene selection, optimize phenotyping protocols for different disease contexts, and validate findings through stable germline mutants. Nevertheless, this work establishes zebrafish crispant analysis as a practical and biologically informative tool for medium-throughput functional screening of FBD candidate genes.
